newsitem.title: UK: UK's Cook gives some support to French jobs call.
newsitem.headline: UK's Cook gives some support to French jobs call.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook on Friday gave qualified support to France's call for employment objectives to be built into the criteria surrounding European economic and monetary union.

Echoing the demands of the new French Socialist government, Cook told the New Statesman magazine he wanted the existing monetary criteria to be supplemented by a judgement on economic growth and jobs.

"When we come to make a decision on joining the currency we will certainly look at the Maastricht Treaty. But we will also look at what will be the impact on industrial growth and jobs, which is our bottom line," he said.

"Macroeconomic management must be balanced by clear objectives for growth and employment," he said. But any new aims could not be introduced at the expense of easing the rigorous budget deficit demands laid out in the Maastricht Treaty.
Cook said the French government had been elected with a mandate rejecting the austerity of the Maastricht criteria and said their views would be cut a little slack as a result.
"In principle, I don't have any disagreement with supplementing the fiscal and monetary criteria with an objective to widen economic policy to take growth and employment into account," he said.

"But this must not be a code for so loosening the criteria that the currency does not become credible. France must decide whether it is making demands which are incompatible with the currency going ahead at all."

French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin was swept into power on June 1. New finance minister, Dominique Strauss-Kahn, immediately met his EU counterparts and told them he could not sign the Stability Pact -- which sets out fines for countries adopting the euro if their budget deficits reach excessive levels.
The French government wants guarantees about employment written into the EMU process, something which Strauss-Kahn said the stability pact did not do.
This weekend, EU leaders meet in Amsterdam for a summit intended to wrap up the intergovernmental conference and produce agreements on how EMU should move forward.
It is unclear whether France will play ball even though Jospin and his president, Jacques Chirac, are meeting German Chancellor Kohl on Friday to try and reach an agreement ahead of the summit.

But on Thursday, Jospin met European Commission President Jacques Santer and said progress was made. And EU sources say France may be satisfied with a new focus on employment through political declarations alongside the budget accord.
Cook's official position is that Britain is unlikely to join a first wave of EMU, scheduled for January 1999. But he also expressed doubts that the process would start on time in any form.
"Of course, Chancellor Kohl has put his reputation on the line for a single currency, but there are other views in Germany," he told the New Statesman.

He noted that Gerhard Shroeder, a leading Social Democrat who may challenge Kohl in elections next year, has publicly called for delay. On Wednesday, Schroeder said it would be better to shelve the launch of the euro if it was not tied to a budget stability pact.
"So there are interesting things occurring on the continent. It would be a rash person who made a firm prediction either way," Cook said.
